On the motion of Hon. W. J. Roche (Minister of the Interior), Bill No. 107, to amend the Dominion Lands Act, was read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Rainville in the Chair.
On section 1-Cancellation and compensation for- improvements.

This Bill contains a large number of details, and it may be that I have been remiss in not following up the work, but I would not like to be compelled to consider all these many details to-day, not having seen them before.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There is no need of going into any of those sections to which my hon. friend objects. We might run over the Bill and see what part is not controversial. There is no other business ready just at the moment.
Has the Bill been available to hon. members in the shape in which it is now laid on the Table.
It has been distributed.
When?
Only to-day.

That bears out my point. I was saying that the Bill contains a large number of details which require careful consideration before hon. members can be in a proper position to assent to or dissent from them. speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No doubt the Minister of the Interior will agree that any of the sections as to which my hon. friend thinks further consideration will be necessary can stand, and the minister can give
his explanations which will assist my hon friend in his consideration.

Under the circumstances, the Bill having just been distributed, it being a Bill of detailed amendment and we not having had an opportunity to compare it at considerable length with the present Act, we shall have to ask you, Sir, to be good enough to read each section.
1. Subsection two of section fifteen of The Dominion Lands Act, chapter twenty of the Statutes of 1908, is amended by inserting after the word "latter" in the tenth line thereof, the words "or to any other person or persons adjudged by the minister to be entitled thereto as dependents of the former holder of the land," and by adding the following at the end thereof:
"The person who may subsequently secure the land, either under entry or by sale or otherwise, may be required to pay any and all amounts due for principal and interest then charged against such land for seed grain, fod- ' der or other relief advanced by His Majesty to the former or any preceding entrant or holder of such land, in such manner as the minister may direct."
Will the minister give an explanation in regard to this amendment?

The members of the
House will see that in the Bill as it has been distributed, in addition to the amendments that the Chairman has just read, there is in one column the reading of section 2 of the present Act and in the oppo-' site column the reading of the section as it will be afteT amendment, the portion that has been added being in darker type. The explanation of the first change is to clothe the minister with authority to order that moneys collected for improvements made by a former entrant shall, instead of being refunded to the said former entrant, be paid to his wife. In many cases of desertion the woman is unable to obtain an assignment from her husband, although it may be shown in some instances that she has advanced money to her husband to effect improvements. As the law now stands, she has no redress.
There may be other cases where it would be advisable to make a refund to the father or mother or some other near relative of the former holder of the land, on proof being furnished that such relative is the person most entitled to receive the money.
The practice of the department, where the wife has been abandoned, is that after she has been abandoned* for two years, she will be allowed to make entry for the land in her own name. At present the practice is that a woman who is allowed entry is supposed to have her residence count from

the date of entry, but we desire to take the opportunity of allowing the woman to have her residence count even before she has received her entry if she has been residing upon the land subsquent to her desertion. This particular provision means that where the husband has made certain improvements under the existing Act, those improvements may be collected from the next entrant. We do not desire to collect from the deserted wife, but to have authority to pay over the value of the improvements to the wife.
Less the amount of indebtedness?

Yes, if there was anything due. The second change is in connection with the advance of seed grain, fodder and relief made in 1914 and 1915. In'
[DOT] some cases the party obtaining the adv .nee failed to complete the duties in connection with his entry, and such entry has been cancelled. In cases of this kind it has been decided that any one taking up the land later on will have to pay the amount of the advance. In every case, a person obtaining entry for cancelled land is required to pay the value of the improvements remaining upon the land at the time he secures the entry. The amount so collected for improvements is applied on the seed grain debt, 'but if the value of the improvements is not equal to the amount of the seed grain indebtedness, the party securing the land is required to make up the remainder of the indebtedness. For instance, we have a lien on the land of any one who received advances from us in 1914 and 1915 under our seed grain distribution. If the homesteader abandoned that land and we had no lien upon it, the next entrant who applies for cancellation would receive a free entry for that homestead. But when we have -a lien upon the land, in order to protect the treasury we insist that whoever takes up the land must assume the indebtedness over and above the value of the improvements.

If I have been able to
correctly gather the purport of the minister's remarks, I would say that the first change with Tegard to the dependents of a homesteader is a very proper one. But there js no doubt in my mind, in regard to the second change, that the charging of the whole indebtedness against the subsequent entrant for an abandoned homestead will in many cases have the effect of preventing the entry from being made. There 	,
are many cases in which a large indebtedness has been incurred on account of seed grain and fodder, and if another bad season occurs this year-and I ami afraid that some parts of the country may be facing a bad season-many homesteads may be abandoned, particularly those on which the Government has a lien. I think the Government would be well advised not to charge against the incoming settler the indebtedness incurred by the previous homesteader in regard to seed grain and fodder relief, beyond the fair value of the improvements upon the homestead, because if more than the value of the improvements is charged against the incoming settler he will to that extent be deterred from taking the homestead. I am quite sure that the amount of the lien will not be sufficient to deter the homesteader in all oases, but I aim equally satisfied that it will be sufficient to deter him in a large number of cases if the indebtedness is greater than the actual value of the improvements. In that case he will foe required to pay for something that he does not get, and there are very many, people, of course, who object very strongly to paying for. something which they do not get, but which somebody else gets. That sentiment, apart from the actual values, will have a serious effect in deterring the reoccupation of abandoned land. If, on the other hand, the Government undertook to collect from the incoming settler the value of the improvements only which the previous homesteader had made, and which the incoming homesteader would have the benefit of, there would be no such impediment to the re-occupation of the land, and the Government would in all probability get all they possibly could get out of the transaction in a large number of cases. That would encourage the re-occupation of the country, and not deter it, as I am afraid it will be deterred by the provision which the minister is placing in the Act.

Unless we take some means of protecting the treasury, we are liable to lose a very large .amount of money. I do not think we should leave any stone unturned to protect the country against such loss when we have at our hand this method of collecting the indebtedness. I do not look at the matter in exactly the same light as my hon. friend, when he says that the subsequent entrant is paying for something that he does not get. In one sense that is true, but the incoming settler does get the land, and land in a thickly settled portion

of the community-and it was here that the distribution of seed grain was made-is more valuable than far-distant homestead land. Our experience thus far would not lead us tc believe that this provision will be a deterrent against the re-occupation of the land. We have had a number of cases where men were only too pleased, in fact volunteered, to pay off the seed grain indebtedness for the privilege of being allowed priority of entry. The land is valuable, though in some cases there are very few improvements. If the improvements were valued at $300 and the indebtedness at $400, the incoming settler pays the $300 for the improvements in any case, and he is then called upon to pay the other $100 in order to release the Government lien. As we have already had many cases where men were only too pleased to assume this indebtedness, I do not imagine this provision will be a deterrent to the re-occupation of the land, and if we do not have such a provision I fear that the country will be liable to a very serious loss.

I have no wish to put the Government in the position of failing to collect indebtedness that is due 'to the country, but I am compelled to take a view very different from the minister's in this matter. The minister speaks of the willingness of the incoming settler to pay off the seed grain indebtedness, and, I presume, the value of the improvements besides.
The indebtedness over and above the value of the improvements.
I do not gather that that is the wording of the section.
He would have to pay for the improvements in any case, and the amount he pays for improvements is applied on the seed grain indebtedness.

I do not think that is made clear in the section. However, the policy of the department is good enough in that particular. The minister speaks of these seed grain liens having been taken in thickly settled districts, where the land is of sufficient value in itself to make it a business proposition for the incoming settler to pay off the lien.
Under such circumstances of course that is the business way for the transaction to go through, but/ I am compelled to take the view that the large majority of those oases aTe not in the thickly settled parts, but aTe rather in the isolated sections, otherwise the men would not have abandoned
the land. The land is worth just as much to the farmer as it is to the incoming settler, as land or as a speculation, and inasmuch as no business lien can be held against the land there is no reason why he should abandon it. The outlying localities, where the pressure of settlement has not given value to the land, are where abandonment will take place largely, and where it is important that the Government should secure re-occupation of the land. In those localities it is very much more important to secure re-occupation and production of the land than it is to secure the repayment of the balance of the seed grain lien. I would not ask the minister to delay this section, because I think its purpose as explained by him is perfectly clear. I have made my protest against the view taken by the minister, and I am willing to have the section pass. At the same time I must contend strongly that the minister has made a statement of the case which, in my judgment, is not generally applicable, and it will not work out as he suggests, but will act as a deterrent to re-occupation and cultivation of the lands.

This legislation was intended to harmonize with our existing practice. I do not know that there have been very many cases of this character, but there have been instances where the applicant for cancellation voluntarily desired to assume the obligations for the sake of getting the land. The laot distribution of seed grain was largely in the south, in the pre-emption area. As the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) well knows, many of those men abandoned the land because of getting into difficulties in other respects, for instance, because of a poor crop, or getting out of their depth financially, or because of indebtedness to implement dealers, merchants, or ^others. Personally I would not be in favour of throwing that land open and losing money, and the only other thing we could do would be to sell the land outright by public auction, to the highest bidder. It is much better to let them get the land free by assuming the seed grain obligation, rather than put it up at public auction with that obligation as the upset price. In the oases which have come before us so far we have been allowing this to he done. I do not anticipate the difficulties my hon. friend (Mr. Oliver) foresees in this regard.

I am aware that has been the practice in the past, and it is because of the instances which have come to my at-



tention thiat I have spoken of. The minister has, no donbt, heard of cases where the incoming settler has come forward and offered to take over the land at that price, but he has not heard of the number of cases where the land has lain vacant year after year simply because of the lien against it, which is a condition very much more detrimental to the welfare of the country than the mere matter of the collection of the balance of the money. Of course, I do not wish to see the money lost if that can be avoided, but neither do I want to see the land kept out of production, or settlement deterred, because of this condition. It very often happens that a business man has to take the -position that the first loss is the best, and that it is better to close the account, take the loss, and start afresh. This is my view in regard to this matter. It is better not to hold the land out of occupation in the hope of collecting the balance of the lien. I admit there are special exceptions, but they are a very small minority.
In regard to the suggestion that the land should be sold for the purpose of realizing the seed grain lien, I would protest most strongly against any such action, because I think it would create a most unfortunate condition of affairs.

How does the hon. gentleman expect the Government will obtain repayment of the money it has lent to the farmer on the security of the farm? Does he suggest the Government should relinquish the security?

Yes. Take the case of a farmer who owns a piece of land which he leases to a tenant on crop payment, and this tenant, by some means or other, finds a means of beating him on the deal. What does he do? He takes the loss and re-leases the land to a man who will produce from it at the first opportunity. He does not hold the land vacant until somebody comes along who will pay him the loss he made through the previous tenant and also assume obligations for the future, which is the position the minister is taking on those abandoned homesteads against which seed grain liens are outstanding. My hon. friend (Mr. Schaffner) would not do it in his own business, and it is not good business for the Government.

The case suggested by my hon. friend is not a parallel one. I could understand the argument in. regard to other debts apart from the Government

loan, but in the case of the seed grain lien, for which the land is security, it is practically money belonging to the state.
Surely.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 2-Holding by husband deemed holding by wife in certain cases:
Will the minister explain that section?

My experience has shown that the department should be given authority to issue patent for a homestead within three years from the date of entry. In the case of a deserted woman, the department grants her an entry upon proof being furnished of not less than two years' time. In the meantime she is required to make the land-for which her husband held entry-her home and also to keep up the improvements. As the law is now constituted, a woman in this position is not entitled to patent until after the expiration of three years from the date she is granted legal entry. Inasmuch as she is required to make the land her home for two years 'before being granted entry, if is desirable that the department should have the right to grant her a patent immediately on proof being furnished thiat she has completed the required six months' residence in each of three years calculated from, date of desertion, in addition to the other requirements of her entry. It seems too bad not to allow the time she has spent doing the duties prior to the date of entry in her own name and therefore we desire to issue the patent three years after the date of desertion.

A person might put in five years on the land, or five years might pass, and if he actually put in six months in three of these years he would be entitled to his patent. The amendment is not limited to the case of :a wife deserted by her husband; it is general in character and it provides that a patent may issue after six months' residence in any three years, not three years immediately preceding the date of entry. Therefore one might go on the land, be in occupation this yeaT, perhaps spend a month on it next year, then go off to work isomewhere else, probably in the United States, come back, remain a little time and the next year after that put in six months, be absent again the following year and the year following that again put in six months. As long as he puts in six months in. one of the three years before he applies for the patent he will get it. If

this amendment were limited to the case o.f a wife who was deserted by her husband I could understand the propriety of it.

Prior to September, 1908,
the practice followed under the Dominion Lands Act permitted settlers to count residence in any one of the following ways:
(1) From' date of entry; (2) from date of commencement of residence either before or after date of entry, or (3) six months' residence in each of three calendar years.
Must they not be succeeding one another?

I do not think that is
compulsory.
(4) Homestead year and calendar year combined, or otherwise shifting the date for the commencement of the term as may be most satisfactory to the settler.
When the Act of 1908 came into force the methods of calculating residence were restricted to the first two.
In some eases a settler, by a technicality is deprived of a portion of his residence, and it is, therefore, desirable that the former method should be re-established, as it is often found that while .a settler may not have performed six months' residence, in each of three years, counted from date of entry or from date of commencement of residence, either before or after date of entry, he- has performed six months' residence in each 'of three years, calculated from some other date than is allowed by the Act of 1908.
This is in effect going back to the practice of the department prior to September, 1908, and it is to deal with cases of hardship where a man through some technicality is deprived of his period of residence by reason of not complying with the existing legislation. We thought it was only right to have this amendment to enable us to revert to the old practice.

I think the amendments go very much farther than my hon. friend has suggested to the committee. Let me compliment the minister on the preparation of the Bill for presentation to the House. It certainly is in very convenient shape for a thorough understanding of its purposes. The explanations and. comparisons are very desirable. But, I desire to make a comparison between subsection (b) of the present Act and subsection (b) of the amended Act as they appear in parallel columns. Subsection (b) of the present Act recites that:	'
241$
To have resided thereon at least six months in each of the three years from the date of entry or date of commencement of residence. _
As it is proposed, subsection (b) will read:
To have resided thereon at least six months in each of three years.
The difference between the two is that there is no fixed starting point as to residence in the new section while there is a starting point provided in the present Act. One As the commencement of residence and the other is the date of entry. Whichever occurs first is the date that will be taken as the basis of the term during which residence must be performed. There is no other conceivable right under which a homesteader can earn a patent than that of his residence or under his date of entry. When these two definite starting points are abandoned there is an uncertainty in the requirements of residence to be met by the settlers which' does not make for the good administration of the Act, for the good settlement of the country, or for the satisfaction of settlers. My hon. friend has spoken of the desirability of there being a greater elasticity in the fulfilment of residence requirements. I agree that it is desirable that there should' be some measure of elasticity, that there should be a considerable amount of discretion left to the administration in that particular. But I maintain that for the satisfaction of the settlers themselves, it is in every way desirable that whatever may occur in regard to the completion of residence duties there should be no uncertainty about the date of commencement. The date of commencement should .be a fixed date for definite reasons as provided in the present Act, namely, it must be the date either of the commencement of residence or the date of entry. I would certainly urge very strongly that to omit that fixity of date is a very great blemish on the Act as it is proposed and will do incalculable damage in deterring the settlement of the country because in the administration of the land there will be cases of dissatisfaction on account of the different treatment that one settler will get as compared with the otheT. The -success of homestead settlement depends largely upon the confidence that the homesteaders have in the granting of the rights that they earn, and in order that there shall be that satisfaction it most be known beyond question what these rights are and when they begin although there must always be a certain amount of discretion left as to the time In

which these duties are completed. I consider that the minister is making a great mistake in making the changes which he proposes in the particulars I have mentioned.

The hon. gentlemen takes it for granted that we are abandoning the two methods in use under the old Act. We are not doing that at all; we are simply adding another option to the terms of residence. Because of cases that have been brought to the attention of the officials of the department in which grave hardships would have been imposed on settlers had the rule been strictly followed of counting the time of residence from the date of entry or the date of the commencement of residence either before or after entry, and in which cases there has been some elasticity in the application of the rule, this amendment has been proposed. We are nor foregoing anything, but simply restoring, in addition to the existing options, the condition that existed before the legislation of 1908.

The minister has a majority and can force the Bill through, and I do not wish to delay its passage. But I point out to him that it was under the provisions of the Act of 1908 that the largest settlement in our history occurred in the Prairie West, and that there was the greatest satisfaction in the relations between the homesteaders and the department. Had there not been such satisfaction there would not have been such extensive settlement. I am not going to ascribe a sinister motive to the minister or to the Administration, but I am going to assert that only sinister results can follow from a condition in which the point of commencement of the rights of the homesteader is left in doubt or in question.
There is no doubt. Why did not those sinister motives exist prior to 1908 when there was similar legislation?

I do not wish to rake up past memories, but the provision of 1908 was adopted because, under the Administration that my hon. friend proposes to revert to, there was dissatisfaction, which had been a deterrent to settlement, and I point out that it was under the changes in the Act of 1908 that the great progress in western settlement was made, showing beyond question that the Act had not been made less adaptable to the conditions, but if anything more adaptable. I am not assuming sinister motives, but pointing out the certainty of sinister results; that when the
'
homesteader goes to the land office and asks for his patent and he does not know when his rights begin, they will begin when the Administration say they ought to begin.
Oh no, they will be published in regulations and sent broadcast.
This is the Act, this is not a regulation, and the Act provides that the settling of points in reference to men's rights shall depend on the judgment of the department.
No.

I shall have to disagree with the minister; that' is what the Act says and provides. That is an unfortunate provision and is bound to lead to dissatisfaction and complaint on the part of settlers who have been treated differently from their neighbours, and who will ascribe such varying treatment to sinister motives, where they consider they have had the worst of the deal. I suggest that the minister leave subsection (b) of section 16, where :t is today. It will not interfere with the exercise of reasonable discretion in the relaxation of conditions when the patent lias to he issued. I say it is bad administration not to make specific provision in the Act so that every man will know exa'cfcly when his rights begin.

To show that there is no sinister motive behind this, I wdl take the hon, gentleman at his word and place the responsibility on his shoulders for any lack of elasticity in the future. My suggestion of this legislation was in order to make it easy for the homesteader, and to give the department a little more elasticity. At present they have the option of 'counting residence from the date of entry or from the date of commencement of residence either before or after entry, and my suggestion was simply to add two other provisions. They would be under the same conditions as the other two, only there would be two more options. But the hon. gentleman thinks there is something sinister behind this, and I am agreeable to leave the section as it is.
I expressly said I did not suggest sinister motives, but I did suggest sinister results.

The people I represent are not now much interested in the working of the Homestead Act as practically all patents have been issued for homesteads in my constituency. But I should not like to see the minister drop this amendment.

I 'think it is perfectly Tight, as it leaves the homesteader all the opportunities he had before to count his residence from the date of entry or from the date when he went into residence on his homestead. He has all the advantages he has had up to the present, and he has one more opportunity, of getting his six months in in each year for three years. He had not that option before and to that extent, in my judgment, the amendment is to the advantage of the homesteader, and I think it should carry.
That was the idea.
I want to say that I probably represent a larger proportion of homestead area than any other member, and in my judgment I would desire that the minister should make the change as suggested.
Is the argument presented by the hon. member for Assiniboia that it gives the homesteader one more advantage, correct? If it is, for Heaven's sake let us give it to him, he has hard times now.

It gives the Administration one more opportunity to grant or withhold, with or without cause, and thereby create dissatisfaction amongst the settlers, and retards settlement. It was 'because of that that the change was made in 1906, and the change was followed toy a stupendous success in the homesteading, net only in the volume of homesteading, but in the satisfaction between the homesteaders and the Government. There was no other period in the homestead history of Canada when there was as much satisfaction between the homesteader and the Government as during that period and under that law. All that I am asking is that that provision, which was placed there for good reasons, toe continued in the interests of the homesteader.

At present, when the
homesteader applies for a patent, he either goes to the land office and interviews the official there, or he gives notice, and the homestead inspector comes to the settler. The officials in the land office and the homestead inspector are all well posted as to just how a homesteader can apply for and secure his patent, and I venture to say there is not one case in ten where the homesteader does not consult with the officials and the inspector, and makes his application as prescribed by these officers. Many of the homesteaders do not understand the regulations absolutely, and it
comes back to the same thing, that this gives the homesteader one more opportunity and it does not take away one single iota of the advantage that he has at the present time. If the regulation governing what is proposed here is published, I do not see that any official of the department can vary it once it is published.

Apparently the views of the hon. gentleman from Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) harmonize with my own views, and I have as much right to pay attention to the views of the hon, gentleman from Assiniboia as I have to pay attention to the views of any other member of the House. I should-like to have his criticism of the section, and also the criticism of other members from the West. I should like to get their opinion on it before consenting to revert back to the former legislation. I have not any strong views myself. I want to do anything I can to aid the homesteader and make it easier for him, whilst imposing the usual duties on him. That is the only object I had in view, and I should like to know just exactly the feeling of the other members from the West with regard to the change I have suggested.

I was not in the House when the discussion commenced, but I do not see why the hon. gentleman from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) is objecting to the amended section. I represent a large number of homesteaders, and I have, time after time, realized that the law as it stood militated against the homesteader, and I for one in this House felt that we should do everything we could to assist the homesteader. The changes are simple, giving the' homesteader another opportunity of making good and performing his work. I think it would be a policy that would be condemned by the homesteaders all through the West, and by every member in this House, if we proposed to do anything at all that would militate against the homesteader, and I should like the hon. gentleman (Mr. Oliver) to reconsider his attitude.

I am unable to find any word in this section that gives the homesteader any right that he does not possess under the previous section, but, by the omission of the words in the previous section, I can see very plainly that those who are in charge of the .administration of the law can take away from the homesteader rights which he might very well think he had, and that is something I do not wish to see. I desire to avoid friction between the homesteaders and the Administration, but

my hon. friend opens the door for such friction by taking out of the law that provision which does not, and cannot in any way, interfere with the rights of the homesteader to get his patent, and which only establishes beyond question the date and place and circumstances under which his rights begin. That is w-hat he is taking away from the homesteader, and that is what I object to. In the constituency I represent, and in the adjoining constituency, one of the hon. gentleman's officials, a land agent, has twice been a candidate in the provincial election. In another constituency in the neighbourhood one of his timber inspectors has been a candidate, and in the constituency I represent one of his timber inspectors was a candidate at the last provincial election, and was supported in his candidature by one of his homestead inspectors. Under tho.se circumstances, while I am not accusing, my hon. friend of sinister motives, he will pardon me if, representing a pioneer community, I have some question in my mind as to taking away 4 p.m. from those pioneers the specific right that they shall date the beginning of their right from a fixed point set down in the Act, and make them dependent on inquiry from the homestead inspectors or the land agent, or the timber inspectors, or some- other officials of this Government, to find out when and where their rights begin.

The hon. gentleman overlooks the fact that there will be no more doubt in the mind of the homesteader under this section than there is at the present day under the old section. This Act is printed and available for any homesteader, and he can read the Act as it will be amended, just the same as he can read the present Act, and the Act gives him the privilege of having four options. He has one option more than provided under the present Act. There is no taking away of any right.
Would the hon. gentleman read the section of the Act with reference to options?

I have read it, but I am
telling the hon. gentleman that he still has the same right

The present Act provides
that the time shall count, (I) from the date of entry, (2) or from the date of commencement of residence, either before or after date of entry. Now we propose to add to that.
Where do you add to it?
We add the words " six months in each of the three years."
Will the hon. gentleman read the paragraph where he makes that addition?

This is the explanation and object of the Act as it will be administered. The explanation of this section reads:
(3)	Six months' residence in each of three calendar years.
(4)	Homestead year and calendar year combined, or otherwise shifting the date for the commencement of the term as may he most satisfactory to the settler.
If this legislation passes it is intended to give these other two privileges in counting the time, in addition to the provision in the existing Act. That is the result of the Act.

My hon. friend has stated that certain intentions of the department in matters of administration are contained in the Act. They are not contained in the Act, and the omission does not interfere with the additional consideration that he suggests he is so ready to give to homesteaders. He takes away from the homesteader the fixed date upon which the homesteader knows by Act of Parliament that his rights begin, and he substitutes nothing for that, except the statement that he is going to administer the Act in a certain way.

Section (b) at present reads:
(b) To have resided thereon at least six months in each of ' three years from the date of entry, or the date of commencement of residence.
The amended section will read:
(b) To have resided thereon at least six months in each of three years.
And that leaves it-
Entirely in the hands of the department to say when it shall begin.

Exactly. The hon. gentleman must take it that the Act will be administered by the officials appointed by my hon. friend's (Mr. Oliver) Government in the best interests of the settlers. The officials the hon. gentleman appointed during his regime are still administering this Act.

I am sorry to eay that that is not absolutely correct. I do not wish to enter into an argument with the minister, but that does not happen xo be true. Mr. LEVI THOMSON. In case, there are children, they would be cut off entirely.

I see there is a difference between the estate of an ordinary homesteader and that of a deceased .soldier where the duties not only of residence but of cultivation are remitted. She generally works the land in place of her husband who has gone to the war.
. Mr. OLIVER: Many of them have not done so but they have suffered deprivations that, entitle them to consideration at the hands of this House. We decided that the best way to deal with the subject was to issue patents at the end of the accustomed period of three years providing all the duties were done, and providing that the homesteader declared his intention of becoming a British subject. Whether, in the opinion of Parliament, it is necessary that
the time should be extended so as not to issue patent until the end of five years, or whether it is necessary to impose a penalty, is of course, another consideration, but even if at the end of thre years we do compel an alien to become naturalized, there is no reason whatever why such person, as soon as be receives his patent, might not dispose of his land to another alien thus leaving the land still in the hands of an alien. If, however, it is considered there is a weakness .in the existing Act, I am open to suggestions, as to the best methods of remedying the same.

I am not criticising from the point of view the minister has indicated, but am stating that in 'administering this Act during the past several years, the department has apparently, by raising impediments, Tefused to give to aliens the benefits of the Act. The alien, for one .reason or another, was not able to get naturalized, and difficulties were thrown in the way of getting his patent, so that he did not get it. Was that an accident, or did it happen by design? What was the policy of the department in the past, and what is to be its policy in the future? Is it to be the policy that an alien-not an alien enemy-on fulfilment of his three years' duties, may get and will he given his patent?

Upon inquiry, I do not
know of any cases of the nature suggested by the honourable gentleman unless the parties were alien enemies During the war, of course, some difficulties have been thrown in the way of alien enemies. In war time, under the War Measures Act, alien enemies cannot secure patent. I am not aware that the department have thrown any difficulties in the way of aliens securing their patents. If the hon. gentleman can bring any such cases to my knowledge, I shall be glad to have them looked into. It is not the policy of the department to throw any obstacles in the way of aliens securing patents.

The policy of the department then is that if the alien has fulfilled his duty, and if he is not an alien enemy, he can get his patent. The other position is that the alien has received the material advantage .of citizenship, although still an alien. What I want ito get at is this: Is there any mutual obligation existing between the alien and the Government on the one part or on the other as a result of this material advantage which the alien has secured?

This has to do with the Naturalization Act which used to give a man the privilege of becoming a citizen after three years' residence The Naturalization Act which is in force in this country now is virtually a subject of treaty with Great Britain, and it extends the time to five years. I suppose the view of the department was to continue to grant the patents at the end of the three-year period, following the American practice. A man has to put in six or eight years' residence in the United States before he can become a citizen. After he goes to the United States and has been resident there for some time, he can take out what is known as his "intention." He can go before a justice of the peace or some other federal officer and subscribe to a declaration that he intends to become a .citizen of the United States, and in that declaration he foreswears allegiance to the country he has left. The federal law will not allow a man to be a captain or to hold a certificate for various things unless he is a citizen of the United States. Some of the States make matters easier. For instance, the state of Michigan declares a man eligible to do everything under the Federal Act, who has made a declaration of his intention and who was a citizen of contiguous territory. That throws the citizenship open to a Canadian. In the state of Washington or some of the other western states, they go so far as to say that if a man makes a declaration of his intention to become a citizen, he is entitled to all the rights of citizenship and can not only hold land but vote. The idea in this Bill is to follow the American practice, and it would enable Americans to obtain title to their land, if they made a declaration of intention at the same time as they applied for their land. They will have to put in three years' residence after that before they can become citizens. I do not think this Parliament has anything to do with whether the term of residence for naturalization is to be three years or five. That was settled with the British House of Commons by arrangement. If a man goes through all the same motions as he would before a justice of the peace when becoming a full citizen, he should get his land just as before he could in three years become a citizen and get his land.

Are those who declare intention to become citizens of the United States liable to be drafted under the law - which has just been put into force there? This question brings up the very point as to whether a person who is an alien and

who has not completed his citizenship duties, while receiving the advantages of citizenship, may not, if an alien, be liable to draft.

I understand that question has been answered in the last day or two in the United States by the statement that they are going to draft all aliens, and if the aliens do not wish to serve, they will be deported. That is a simple method of settling the problem.

Under this law, the alien gets the benefit of all homestead rights. I understand from the minister very definitely that it is not the intention or part of the policy of the Government to withhold in any degree his homestead once he has earned it according to the terms of the law. He is on an absolute equality with every other man. Am I correct in that?
Yes.
Does this declaration of intention make the homesteader subject to obligations to the state other than are imposed on any other alien?

Obligations as to military
service?	.
Take that, for instance.

I should not like to give an opinion offhand on such a delicate point as that. It has never been brought to my attention before, and has nothing whatever to do with the administration of the Dominion Lands Act. I really could not say definitely whether or not he would be amenable to our Military Service Act.

I think it has everything to do with the administration of the Dominion Lands Act. It is a fundamental principle of the Dominion Lands Act that we do not give our free land to anybody unless and until he is ready to assume all the obligations of citizenship. That was the fundamental principle of the homestead law during all the years previous to 1914, and I want to know if that principle is being absolutely departed from-or is there some saving provision that will protect the public interest in that regard? It is a matter of very great interest to know whether the man to whom we have given all the privileges of citizenship in our power, as regards the ownership of land, renders himself liable, for instance, to military service to the state. Does this declaration of intention bring him under any such obligation in any way?

This discussion suggests to me that perhaps we had better revive our three-year citizenship, which was' a citizenship as regards Canada only. We have now a five-year citizenship, which is a citizenship in the British Empire. I can see there is a hiatus here between the three years and the five. We may have gone too far in doing away with our three-year citizenship, as regards' the imposing of the obligations of citizenship on those who obtain free-grant lands from this country.

I do not think that can be changed, but the man could take an oath that he would take out his citizenship papers at the end of five years, and he could at the same time obligate himself not to claim citizenship in any country in the meantime. He could take oath that he would be amenable to all the laws of the state, military service included; in other words, he could take oath that he would become a citizen or assume all the obligations of citizenship. Then, if at the end of the five years, he did not take out his papers as he had sworn to do, he could be punishable under the Criminal Code for having taken a false oath.
I do not think any court would prosecute a man who in an affidavit expressed an intention to do'some act in the future.

He swears definitely that he will take out his papers at the end of five years; that is taking an oath, not expressing an intention. The oath taken in the United States is very, very rigid. Not only does he declare his intention of taking out papers, but at the same time he foreswears any citizenship that he at that time holds. I have seen lots of copies of the oath of intention in the United States; they can be seen in the Library here. The declaration of intention is a solemn oath that from that minute forward the man forswears-not that he is going to forswear, but forswears then and there-all his privileges as a citizen in any other country, and more particularly, he takes an oath against the sovereign of the country to which he at that time belongs. So it is a most solemn oath. I >. should think that if a man obtains under false pretenses all the rights of citizenship as regards free land, he could be punished under the ordinary law of the land if he took such an oath falsely.
I think my hon. friend should study the law before he attempts to lay down legal propositions.
What is the law on this point?

I do not think you can prosecute a man for false declaration of intention. I have had some experience myself, and I know positively that you cannot prosecute a man for obtaining anything under false pretenses, if the false pretenses relate to the future. It would he impossible to prosecute a man for obtaining his homestead under false pretenses in the way that my hon. friend suggests. There may be some other way of doing it-and I am merely throwing this out by way of suggestion. It seems to me that rather than go through all the rigmarole suggested by the hon. member for Simcoe, we might better adopt the suggestion of the hon. member for Saskatoon and revert to our old plan of three-year citizenship for this particular case. We might allow Candian naturalization only-not British citizenship-to the person who required it for the purpose of taking out his homestead patent, or we might provide a penalty in case the homesteader failed to take out naturalization papers within a reasonable period after the time set. It seems to me there should be some compulsion on a man who gets the benefits of Canadian citizenship, and refuses to carry out his undertaking to the department given in the agreement conferring on him those benefits.

There appears to be a
weakness in our existing law in that one point. The Act, of course, was passed when no war was in sight. I think perhaps the besit way out of the difficulty might be for the man to obligate himself, in the declaration of intention, to discharge the duties of citizenship, and penalties could he provided in case of his failure to do so.

What is the position in
regard to alien enemy homesteaders? I have no doubt that many homesteaders of alien enemy nationality have taken up land and were continuing to take up land until they were prohibited by the order in council in December last.

Under the order in council, which was passed under the authority of the War Measures Act, no alien enemy is now allowed to secure a homestead entry, but those who had secured homestead entry prior to the passng of the order in council are allowed if, tbev can eet naturalized in the meantime, to secure their patents. We did not think it right, when they had made their entry under normal conditions and ac-



cording to the regulations, to withold the patent if they could get naturalized.
I suppose a man of alien enemy nationality would have to reside in the country for five years before he could become naturalized and before he could get his papers?
Three years, up to the end of this year. There were some who had made entry prior to the passing of that Naturalization Act, and the time will expire at .the end of this year.
Until the passage of the order in council no distinction was made between a homesteader of alien enemy nationality and a man who is only an alien?
No.

I wish to be very clear on that point, because I am afraid there have been impediments thrown in the way of such men getting their patents, even after they had fulfilled their duties, and I assumed it was the policy of the department. I did not discuss it with the department, of course, but from the difficulties that were raised it seemed to me that possibly the department had a policy on the subject and did not intend to give patents to homesteaders of alien enemy nationality.
Not unless they become naturalized.

Then I am to understand from the minister that the man of alien nationality who entered for a homestead in good faith previous to the order in council prohibiting such entry is treated just the same as anybody else?
Except that he has to be naturalized.
The man of alien enemy nationality must be naturalized before he gets a patent, and he can be naturalized on a three years' residence?
Yes, under the law at present, and up to the end of this year. ,

speechtext:
So far as I am concerned, and I think I speak tor the soldier in the trenches, we deeply resent the conduct of the people at home who will pander to these alien enemies and will permit them to take up the rights of citizenship when they are of military age and when they still hold their citizenship in Germany and Hungary, and where there is no law which compels them to forswear their allegiance to those countries. I deeply regret that this country has not seen fit, so far, to take the same action as has been taken by all the other Allies with regard to aliens, and to see' that they are deprived of the rights to become citizens during the war. We are at war, and if we do not disturb them or take their property away from them, it is simply because we view these matters with justice. Persons of British origin who owned property in Germany have had their property taken away from them and have been locked up in jail. Dr. Boland, a member of this House, has been treated in that way, and why? Because ihe happened to be a Canadian. I say again that those men who are colonized in the various constituencies of the West, who are of military age and who are alien enemies, have no right to the privilege of citizenship during the war, and I protest most strongly against this Government or any other Government giving them the rights of British subjects while war is on. I do this feeling that I am expressing the views of the men who are fighting the battles of Great Britain, and Canada, and who are trying to play the game on the square, and who do not like this crooked political game going on in different sections of this country. Our men are giving this country and the Mother Country all that is best in them. They are willing to sacrifice their blood, their lives, and while they are fighting in the trenches in Flanders this country goes on making citizens of Germans and Hungarians who are of military age and who are reservists in the German, Austrian and Hungarian armies. I protest with all my force against that, and I say this House should take action before it	closes to see that
those	of alien	enemy birth	who
have been given the rights of citizenship should be restrained from voting during the war; ot, in other words, from putting their' arms up against the men who are at the front because there is not one of these men in the West, who, if given the right to vote, would not vote against any candidate who was friendly to this war or to our soldiers. It is all right 242J
enough to talk, but I have met these Germans at very close quarters and I know them. I am just as willing to fight the German reservist right heTe as I am to fight the German soldier on the plains of Flanders. He is most dangerous at home. I protest, in the name of the soldiers at the front, against permitting these aliens to exert any hostile influence on behalf of our enemies. In the name of heaven, what right have these men to raise their hands and use thete votes against the men in the trenches as they are about to do? I cannot see any difference between the man across the river, in Quebec, who is against conscription and comes out in the open and says: I want a referendum before conscription is put in force, and the man who sits in this House and says: I will vote for conscription but I want to come back to this House with the votes of the German reservists or the Huns. That is straight talk and it might as well come out here as anywhere else. I believe that I speak on behalf of the man at the front who is ready to lay down his life, and I say that it is an insult to him that this House of Commons should pander to the votes of aliens of this description who are being made British citizens and whose votes fob winning the war may overbalance the votes of the soldiers at the front. I call upon this House, I call upon the minister, to see that none of these aliens are granted their land until after the war is over. They would not be citizens in their own country entitled to vote, so we are not taking away from them anything they would have in their own country. Nor, would they he able to take land in their own country unless they belonged to a certain select class. Therefore we are not taking anything away from them in that respect. Many hon. members of this House, who are fond of declaring themselves to be supporters of soldiers and returned soldiers, especially hon. gentlemen on the opposite side of this House, take the stand that these aliens are entitled to take possession of their lands, be naturalized and vote. Those who should be citizens and entitled to take land and vote in Canada should not be alien enemies.

I did not expect that the Naturalization Act would come up for discussion while the Dominion Lands Act was under consideration. At the present time alien enemies are not allowed to make entry for land in Canada and they have not been allowed to do so since the passage of the order ip council under the War Measures Act. The question' of issuing naturali-

zation certificates is one that is within the discretion of the courts. Some judges have taken the view that aliens, when they applied for certificates of naturalization, were entitled to have those certificates issued, in the usual order of things, in peace times as in war times. On the other hand, Chief Justice William Meredith took the position that he would not issue a certificate of naturalization during war time. It is a matter of discretion with the judges as to whether naturalization should be conferred upon an alien enemy during war time or not. After this year that will disappear and the Government will have more jurisdiction in the matter. At the present time it remains with the courts to exercise their discretion but under the proposed amendment of the Naturalization Act the judges will refer the matter to the Secretary of State and he will have jurisdiction over the question as to whether a certificate of naturalization shall be issued or not.

There is a great deal in what my hon. friend (Mr. Currie) has said that I do not agree with. We invited people to come to this country from different countries of the world. A great many Austrians, Galicians and Germans came into Canada. They came on our invitation and on our agreement that if they did certain things we would do certain things. They were promised that if they came in they would be allowed to get a quarter-section of land as a homestead on a payment of $10 entry fee, and that if they lived .on the land for six months each year for three years and applied for their naturalization papers,

they would get their naturalization papers, become British subjects, Canadian citizens, and would also get the patent for their land. I do' not believe that the fact that war has been forced upon the world by the ruler of one of the countries from which these people come is a sufficient reason why Canada should adopt the German principle and make a treaty, of a bargain, simply a scrap of paper to be burned up whenever it suits one's purpose to do it. The Austrians, the Galicians, the Polanders-the bulk of those people would not go back if they could go back; you could not force them to go back. They came away from these countries to avoid being conscripted and forced into war whether they wanted it or not. That does not apply to the same extent to the Germans; I agree that some of them would go back. But a very considerable number of Germans from the West are to-day fighting in the Canadian ranks, on the Canadian side. When I was in the West within the last month, I came across one man who>
was bom in Germany, who has been out here for a number of years, a man 33 or 35 years of age, married and with a family of children. This man's father and mother are in Saskatchewan. His mother cannot speak any English, and his children cannot speak any German. That man's two younger brothers enlisted in a Canadian regiment in the town of Oxbow, and they are in the trenches to-day fighting for Canada and for the British Empire. I ask any member if he would disfranchise these men and their brothers and their fathers. There aj;e many such cases. I saw a statement some time ago that six per cent of the voluntary enlistments in Canada were foreigners. I do not mean to say that six per cent hi them were foreigners from enemy countries, but a very considerable percentage were. I know quite a large number in my own constituency, of Germans and Austrians, Germans chiefly, who have gone to the front with Canadian regiments. It is quite probable that it is advisable now to so change the law that men from these countries will know that if they come into Canada they will not have the same privileges as they would have had if they had come earlier. But to enact a law now that shatters the arrangement we made with them, that goes back to our agreement with them, I think would be very poor policy. We hear a great deal in this country about living in harmony and about conciliation-well, well, that is not the way to bring that about. If Great Britain had taken that stand in
South Afriea we should not have had South Africa to-day as one of the strong pillars of the Empire. The one thing that has made Great Britain the greatest colonizing power in the world is that she has treated people from all parts of the world well and fairly, and has carried out her agreements with them, whatever those agreements may have been, and 1 do not think the Government would be justified in breaking an agreement that they made with these people who happened to come from countries with which we are now at war.

I will answer the hon., gentleman in one or two words. He, in common with a great many others who are pandering to the pro-German vote in the West are going about this country saying: Oh, we made an agreement with these poor people; they come under a special agreement with the Government, and we must do this and that for them; it does not do to break an agreement. I want to tell the hon. gentleman that, so far as civil contracts are concerned, there is not a contract in this country with an alien enemy that holds during the war. That is the law. Why should we place a weapon in the hands of these men in the West, as we are doing day by day, whereby they are going to strike down the men in this House and those people in this country who are sending their sons and brothers to this war? There is no law that I have ever been able to discover, international of otherwise, that justifies a course of that kind. I am very pleased that the hon. gentleman got up in his place to defend pro-Germanism in the West. I am sure that I, in common with a great many other people in this House, are not being very greatly amused, but very greatly alarmed, at the extent of the movement that has recently been organized in Canada for the purpose of destroying the historical Conservative party and putting in place of that party a so-called Unionist party. Does this new party hold the same views as the hon. gentleman?
May I-

I beg your pardon. Let me speak and after I have: finished the hon. gentleman can make a speech if he pleases. I was going to say a great movement is organizing, with many newspapers subsidized from one end of the country to the other to bolster up a Union Government. We will all welcome a Government of any kind in this country, call it what you like,

that will end this wai; one day sooner, or save one life, but I, in common with others who have done a little (bit for the w.ar, dread that this may be -a wooden horse that has been saddled and prepared, inside of which we may find something like 40,000 or 50,000 pro-German votes in the West which are going to send down forty or fifty members to support us in this House in carry- ' ing on the war. I cannot see anything like win the war in that. I say that, so far as I am concerned, as a soldier I denounce any attempt to pander to these Germans in the West, and that any man who stands up in this House or on the hustings in this country to advocate that these Hun reservists should have votes or should have any rights except those of minors is deserving of condemnation. They should not have the full rights of British citizens during the war. I say without any reservation that I have no confidence in any man who stands up in this House and says that they should have those rights,
, nor in any man who is a supporter of a propaganda in this country to win the war, for which apparently there are millions of dollars. May I Ibe permitted to suspect very much where that money is coming from. Why, pray, should any British gold be spent to get German votes in the West to send members to this House? What is the object? When the hon. member went to the West years ago there was one tribe of Indians up there called the Blackfeet, and often when they were on the warpath they turned their snowshoes so that if a scout of the enemy ran across their tracks he would think they were travelling in the opposite direction to that in which they were going. I have travelled long enough in politics in this country not to be deceived when any individual or parties turn their snowshoes.
I wish to correct the hon. gentleman-the Blackfeet did not use snow-shoes.
What did they use?
Ponies.

It was the ponies, I acknowledge it. Perhaps it was another tribe that used to turn their snowshoes and so try to deceive people as to the direction in which the warpath was being taken. That cannot go On in this country. No win the war party can pander to the votes of Hun reservists, and I say this so far as my party is concerned, even if I speak alone, and so far as any man in the Liberal party is con-
TMr. Currie.]
cerned who wishes to see the war end, I say it is our duty to take .cognizance of everything peculiar that is going on and to stand to our arms to-day in defence o<f this country and our soldiers, and in condemnation of those who stand up in this House or elsewhere and support the Germans voting in this country or having the right to be made citizens of this country or of exercising any political influence during the war.

My hon. friend need not undertake to lecture me in this House. I am supporting the war as much as my hon. friend is, and the Germans of my constituency will support me in supporting the war. There are not many in my constituency, but those that are there will support the war. I have Germans in my constituency who went across with the first contingent to fight for Canada; and they are fighting there still.
Mr. (CURRIE:	I want to tell the hon.
gentleman that every German who went over with the First Contingent, -and I believe every man of German birth who has yat gone over, has been detained in England or else has been sent back here. With very few exceptions, unless they had the special (permission and authority of the minister, they were not allowed to go to the front. There are no men of German birth in the trenches. I know of only one man of German birth from Canada who entered the trenches, and he was a young man from Stratford, Kahn, or from that district. To tell me what I know is (absolutely not right and absolutely not true- that these men of German birth, German reservists, are sent over to the front to fight in the trenches-it is inconceivable: they cannot get within twenty miles of the trenches. The hon. gentleman says that, because there is an exception, because a few of these men have gone over to England where they are under observation, we should take the whole lot of these reservists to our bosom, and all that sort of thing-and let them vote. We have the evidence plainly before us in the late provincial election that, in the province from which he comes, every one of these Huns has his knife out for the Conservative party and the win-the-war party. He cannot stand up and tell me otherwise, because I know it, 'and I say it is no reason, because some Germans have enlisted and gone over to the war-because there are two or three exceptions of that kind-that we should shut our eyes. A few exceptions do not

prove the case. In fact, the hon. gentleman gave his own case away when >he said the Germans would go over and fight against us if they had a chance. Still he wants them to vote against our -soldiers. There is no distinction in this country between Germans and Hungarians. We no w learn with 'astonishment 'that if a German has resided for three years in this country he can get his citizenship papers and vote at the next election. I -appeal to hon. gentleman of this House: do you think it is fair and right to our soldiers? Do not you think it is an insult to the men you have sent to the front? If you do this, you will put it in the hands of German alien enemies to snipe our soldiers in the hack. That is what they will do.

I was going to say to
my hon. friend that, although the hon. gentleman from Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) does not hold exactly the same views with regard to the measure passed the other day in this House as I do, I resent, as every hon. member in this House should resent, the insinuation of my hon. friend (Mr. Ourrie), when he said a moment ago that the member for Assiniboia was defending pro-Germanism in the West, when everybody knows that his son died for the cause a few months ago. I hope the hon. gentleman will withdraw.
I saw a wounded German-Canadian come back to this country, and I have seen his father, a German, deny him admission to his house. The son, if alive, would disown him.

The hon. member for
North Simcoe is a gentleman, and I think he should withdraw the statement he made with regard to the hon. gentleman from Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff).

It is my word against
the word of the hon. gentleman from Assiniboia. I say be is supporting the German party, the Hungarians and the Germans of the West, in this House, and that he stands for them, and that he thinks they should have the same citizenship and rights as the Canadian who is fighting in the trenches, and I say he is wrong and the people will not support him.

The hon. gentleman
said that the hon. member for Assiniboia defended pro-Germanism, which is quite a different thing.

I am glad the hon. member for North Simcoe said there were some exceptions, because I was going to tell
him that I knew one who, not only was in France, bust was severely wounded, and was just as brave a young fellow as ever stood in clothes.

And those very men
would be the first to vote for and support what I suggest.
Progress reported.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
This fund of $101,000
was created last year, and voted in the Estimates for the year 1916-17, for the purpose of bringing under one service all the preventive officers of the different branches of the department. Most of our preventive officers were temporary employees, who had been paid up to the moment of their permanent employment, out of the contingencies account of the excise! weights and measures, and food branches.
There have been appointed to date, in that service, about 106 preventive officers, who had been on the temporary list of officers for several years past, some as long as fifteen' years. The average salary of these officers is to $950 per year; therefore, the sum necessary to pay them reaches $100,700.
This service is still in the course of organization, and there are still about sixty-four temporary officers, receiving a total salary of a little over $51,000. A large proportion of these officers will be appointed permanently in the near future, to complete the organization, and a certain number will be dismissed as excise work diminishes on account of prohibitory laws.
Nearly, all these are temporary officers. Most of these temporary officers are, at present, employed in the Excise Service. It has been the policy of the department to transfer these officers to the preventive service, when they can be spared from excise.
The department has under consideration at present, the project of embossing promissory notes, checks, etc., with the two-cent stamp, free of charge. At present these commercial instruments are embossed by the British American Bank Note company,
at the cost of $1 per thousand, when an order is above 15,000, and $1.50 per thousand, when undeT that figure, with a minimum charge of $5. The Banker's Association claim that they should- not be called upon to pay the cost of embossing the checks, apy more than the consumer is called upon to pay the printing of the war stamp. The department is inclined to favour the request of the Banker's Association. If the project is brought into practice, it will be necessary to purchase five or six embossing machines. Each machine will have to be manned by an officer skilled in the work of this nature, and additional employees, besides the operator, will be necessary. The salary required, undeT that heading, would probably amount to about $15,000. As this is an entirely new undertaking for the department, it has been thought advisable, for the present, to pay the salaries in connection with this additional staff of the stamp branch of the department, out of this preventive service fund. Therefore, the $54,000 of an increase, under this heading, is to cover the payment of the additional permanent preventive officers to be appointed, and also the salaries of the new stamp staff.
That this new preventive service has proven effective is apparent by a comparison of the revenue from the war stamp duty, and from the excise duty on tobacco and cigars. The preventive service within the last two years was instructed to see to a strict application of the tobacco laws and regulations, a matter which had received but little attention in the past.
Moreover, after the Special War Revenue Act was introduced, the department undertook a campaign of education, which lasted several months. Then it became evident that this law tvas being violated by a very large number of druggists and merchants, without any excuse whatever, and the dis-covry of violations of the law.

I have used the expression " War Fund " because the $125,000 item! in the estimates is: called the "War Fund," in my department. This fund is generally known as the "War Fund " in the department, and, on account of the error I have mentioned, seeing that we had not enough money to meet the expenditure, we were authorized by the Auditor General to take a sum of $27,000 from that war fund.

speechtext:
From what my hon. friend has just said, we would have spent last year more money than we had. speechtext: It is because the service is permanent now. We wanted an amount to pay the permanent service. That is something new that we did not have last year.

I wish to call the atten tion of the Minister of Finance to this item, " Preventive service-salaries, $155,000." That sum is being asked to cover the salaries of preventive service officers, as against $101,000 a year ago. The Minister of Inland Revenue tried gallantly to defend the item, but he will admit that it is no1 defence. It is election gold, and nothing else. Here we are asked to vote this year $54,000 more than last year for the preventive service of the country, when my hon. friend is coming before Parliament with this legislation imposing a new burden on the people of a most drastic nature. The item may not appear very large to my hon. friend, but if so, it is because at the present day he is dealing with millions and hundreds of millions. But the item will strike the popular imagination as a large amount, and it is by pruning away such useless expenditure, such election expenditure, that my hon. friend will really be what he ought to be, the faithful watchdog of the treasury. We are living in extraordinary times. We are asked, day in and day out, to pay from our income in order to maintain our position at the front and help the Allies to win the war, and this should be the primary consideration of the Government. I said yesterday, when my hon. friend introduced his income tax resolution, that I considered it was a logical sequence of our entering into this war, that while I would approve of the measure, yet the public and the taxpayers of this country would expect that the chief tax gatherer would cut off all unnecessary expenditure. We are this evening discussing an item which is not a very important one, I confess, but looking at the figures for the preventive service salaries this year, we are asked to vote $155,000 as against $100,000 last year. The minister has explained that with this $54,000 additional he would, if need be, pay extra officers. Now we are not in a mood to accept such a vague

explanation, and the people will not listen to such a lame explanation. Extravagance is always to be condemned, but if, perchance, extravagance had to be condoned, and not condemned, it would be whilst we were in prosperous times, when there was no war, when the Government did not require to have recourse 10 p.m. to drastic taxation measures. Surely, Mr. Chairman, I expect from my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White), in whom 1 have,
I must say, some confidence-I should even say, much confidence-better things. It is true he has erred; it is true that he is not with the party with whom he was long associated. I believe he has erred, but I believe that he is honest, that he means [DOT] well, and that at the present time he is doing his best to weather the storm which has gathered around him. I appeal to him, and I am in earnest and sincere about it. The hon. gentleman is taxing right and left, he is taxing the war profiteers, and he has done well in doing so. He is taxing,
I hope, the gentlemen, the patriots who were so sternly rebuked by the officer of the Government, Mr. O'Connor, the other day. He is taxing the common people. The income tax will reach the common people, and the country is patriotic enough to accept those taxation measures, but with some apprehension, I must confess. The country is so patriotic that there is no revolution in sight.
