I said yesterday that you could reduce by fifty per cent the ordinary expenditure of the Government until the war was over, and I stick to my statement, and I say that here is one instance where my hon. friend should cut off this $54,000, which is an absolutely useless expenditure.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I must confess
that I am somewhat overwhelmed by this unexpected compliment by my hon. friend from Rouville. I think there must be something very peculiar in this case, when he finds it necessary to resort to such an unaccustomed and such an unusual course as that which he has pursued. He has stated that the Government might cut the ordinary expenditure of the Dominion in

half. He might just as well have said that we could cut it down to 25 per cent of the present amount. There would be just as much truth in the one statement as in the other, for a statement that the Dominion Government could cut down the expenditure toy one-half is simply an absolute absurdity. Since the war has broken out the Dominion Government, as a Government, and myself, as Finance Minister, have endeavoured in every way possible, so far as the ordinary expenditure and the capital expenditure of this country is concerned, to keep within the closest possible bounds, because we have been awaTe of the burden which the war has imposed and will impose upon us.
I need not go into figures, but I can make this general statement, that, except in so far as the Dominion Government was committed on capital expenditure so that withdrawal would mean heavy loss in work partially completed and in contracts that had been entered into, we have in every way possible reduced our expenditure. There is a matter in connection with our war time expenditures that is not appreciated in this House. It is generally assumed that all ordinary expenditure should be reduced. Upon many of the departments, apart altogether from the wrr, the expenditure has necessarily been increased, the cause indirectly being the war. In addition to that, we must remember that the trade of this country is double what it was before the war, and that means that the public services of this country have had to rise to the occasion. Take the Post Office Department. Does any one mean to suggest that with the enormous volume of business that is being done to-day the expenditure of the Post Office Department could or should be decreased? The other day, when I had the Civil Service Bill before the House, the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) and others protested that we did not pay the 'Civil Service of this country enough. Now we hear to-night that we should cut the expenditure in half. The expenditure of the Post Office Department is necessarily increased by reason of the increased volume of business. My hon. friend is thinking of 1911 and 1910, when the trade of this country was $750,000,000. To-day we are confronted with a situation in which the trade of this country is $2,000,000,000. All the departments administering the Government's functions in connection with that trade naturally have an increase in their expenditure. Take the enormous revenue we are deriving from the Customs Depart-

nient to-day as compared with 1914, or
1910,	or 1911. Does anybody say that there should be a reduced staff in the Customs Department today, seeing that it is swinging the volume of business it does? You cannot expect .a reduction. The same is true of the other departments. Take my own department. The other day the question was asked, no doubt to make it do service on the election platform: How many employees had you in 1911, and how many employees have you to-day? The answer which I gave indicated that we had considerably over 100 more temporary employees in the department than we had in
1911,	.and the statement is sent out to the country that the Department of Finance has over 100 more employees than it had in 1911. Of course, we have over 100 more employees, and if we had'an. additional fifty, we would not have too many to handle the volume of work in the department in connection with the war loans of the Dominion. The administration of the department has necessarily been increased. I had to create .a staff throughout all Canada for the purpose of administering the Business Profits War Tax Act. I had to have a commissioner in every province to represent myself, and those men, had to have with them assistants for the purpose of administering the Act. Does the Dominion lose anything-does the taxpayer of tlie country lose anything-by reason of the fact that we have created a staff for the administration of the Business Profits War Tax Act? Is it good business or *bad that we should spend $100,000 in the administration of the Act, and as a result of the taxation take in for the Dominion of Canada twenty, twenty-five or thirty million dollars a year? The Minister of Inland Revenue has explained to the House the item for preventive officers. What does he want preventive officers for?

What explanation
has he given?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I was not in at
the time, but I know what explanation he would give, because I know the only explanation lie could give.

He has not given
any.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The only explanation he could give is that they were required for the purposes of his department.
He did not say that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The very fact
that the item, is in the estimates indicates that they are required.
My hon. friend is wrong.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: How am I wrong?
The Minister of Inland Revenue is not asking for $54,000; he is asking for $155,000 as against $101,000 a year ago, when the War Tax Act was in force. There is an increase of $54,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Let us assume that that is so. The Minister of Inland Revenue estimates that he will require that amount because it is necessary to protect our revenue further than it is protected at the present time. Why does the Minister of Customs appoint additional officers? He appoints them because they are required in connection with his department, to safeguard the revenue of the Dominion. The same thing is true of the Minister of Inland Revenue. My hon. friend (Mr. Lem-ieux) is beside the mark when he speaks of voting $54,000 for the purpose of promoting the political ends of this Government, because that is not the fact; it is not true.
' My hon. friend should be reasonable in his criticism. This $54,000 will not necessarily be expended unless it is required.

My hon. friend is manufacturing an explanation for the Minister of Inland Revenue. He has indulged in one of his flights of eloquence about the war and other subjects which have no relation under Heaven to the explanations which we have been endeavouring to secure from the Minister of Inland Revenue in regard to this matter. What we have been trying to get from the Minister of Inland Revenue is some explanation why he wants $87,000 more than last year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Will my hon. friend allow me to suggest to him that I was answering a direct question asked me by the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) and a direct criticism which he passed upon the ordinary expenditure of this Government, and that I confined myself absolutely to the point at issue which he raised in his speech?
Then am I to understand that the Minister of Finance was not undertaking to help the Minister of Inland Revenue out of a dilemma?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Minister of Inland Revenue required no assistance from me. I was answering the hon. member for Rouville.

Beautiful, beautiful! For the last two hours we have been endeavouring to get some intelligible explanation from the Minister of Inland Revenue of the increase in the expenditure of his department. He has already given

us three or four different explanations, and at this moment I defy any hon. gentleman in this House to tell us why this increase was made. The minister gave us as one explanation that last year the accountant of his department made a mistake and the expenditure had to be made up from the war fund. The predecessor of the Minister of Inland Revenue, on whose behalf the Minister of Finance would no doubt have talked just as eloquently as he has to-night, last year had an increase of $28,000 over the year before, and, speaking on this item, said:
The department is creating a new fund so as to bring the preventive service under one heading. The creation of this fund does not occasion an increase because certain amounts are taken from other funds, such for instance as the appropriation in connection with the adulteration of food.
Now either the accountant made a mistake last year or he did not, and if the explanation of the Minister of Inland Revenue is correct, then the remarks of the Minister of Finance are wholly irrelevant. Who was the official that made this mistake, and how did the mistake occur? I find that this matter was before Parliament last year at the time Mr. Patenaude was in charge of the department. The Minister of Public Works also took part in the discussion, and if, after the full and free discussion that was had then, the accountant again made such a mistake, all I can say is that you have a pretty state of affairs in the Inland Revenue Department.
Talking about the war does not do away with the absolute necessity of hon. gentlemen finding out what was the reason for the statement made by the Minister of Inland Revenue as to the error made by the accountant. Let us know what the facts are. The minister says on account of this error $50,000 was taken out of the war fund.
Mr, SEVIGN.Y: Not $50,000, tout $27,000; I have said that more than three times already.

My hon. friend went on to say:
I am informed by the officers of my department that last year an error was made by the accountant of the department in making an estimate of $101,000, and that we have had, on account of that error, to make an expend!, ture from the War Fund. It is to meet the exigencies of the service that we ask for $155,000 this year.
That is what the Minister of Inland Revenue stated in this House only four weeks ago. He says now that it was only $27,000.

If that is true, why does he want this $28,000 (more. The minister should give us some intelligible explanation as to what he is going to do with the $54,000 increase over what his predecessor asked the House for last year. We have no objection on this side of the House to the minister getting his estimates through, bu.. let us have some sensible explanation of a condition of affairs which my hon. friend himself says exists.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
The increase asked for
by my department this year is $57,000.

Pardon me-$87,000;
made up of $3,000 for preventive service contingencies, $54,000 preventive service salaries, and $30,000 travelling expenses, etc.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: My hon. friend will remember that in February last an amount of $30,000 was voted by the House for my department.
That makes $117,000 of an increase this year.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
That amount of $30,000
was voted for 1916-1917, so that only leaves an increase of $3,000 for contingencies, and $54,000 .for salaries, or $57,000 altogether.
The $30,000 that was voted was for travelling expenses?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
Last year $60,000 was
voted for travelling expenses, rent, fuel, stationery, etc. When the department saw that that amount was not sufficient, we decided to take $27,000 out of the $125,000, with the approval of the Auditor General, to pay the preventive officers. Before doing that, the accountant of my department had a consultation With the Auditor General and was advised that there was nothing wrong in arranging matters that way. The officers were doing the .same work that is covered by this item for stamps, stationery, salaries, travelling expenses, etc., in connection with war tax. When the accountant of my department, who is a very good official, saw that he had the authority of the Auditor General he had no scruples about taking this amount of $27,000 out of the $125,000. This year, in February, we asked Parliament for the sum of $30,000 to pay the expenses of 1916-17, that is last year, and the amount was voted. This year there is an increase of $57,000 over the amount voted last year, and out of this $57,000 it is the intention of the department to organize a plant to emboss cheques, which it is estimated will cost about $25,000. That leaves
a balance of about $32,000 of an increase for this year.
It is all very well for my hon. friend to say that the expenditure of the department is increasing all the time, but he should not forget that the revenue of the department is also increasing. In the preventive service as organized by my department there was an increase in revenue of $1,500,000 last year. Now I put it to the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald), is it not wise to spend $50,000 ot $100,000 if by so doing we can increase the revenue by $1,500,000? Competent officials of my department assure me that next year they anticipate an increase in revenue of $2,000,000, instead of $1,500,000. Under these circumstances I think it is only reasonable and businesslike to make the expenditure asked for in these estimates.

The pyrotechnics indulged in by my hon. friend, and which he has learned from his colleague, have no relation whatever to this item. My hon. friend has a. separate item covering the payment of salaries of officers and inspectors of excise, who collected the extra money that came into that department, and there is an increase of $5,442,50 in that item.
But my hon. friend's explanation is that in the item of travelling expenses, rent, fuel, and stationery-for which $60,000 was added last year-he spent $27,000 more, and that was the money which he says he took out of the item in connection with the war tax. He told us earlier in the evening that it was on account of extra salaries paid to extra officers, and now he tells us that the $27,000 was on this item for which he is asking $90,000, namely, travelling expenses, rent, fuel and stationery. It is clearly evident that my hon. friend thought he would follow the example of his colleague, but he was entirely out of touch with his explanations, because he was paying travelling expenses, rent, fuel and stationery, and he paid $27,000 more last year than his people estimated. If his explanation helps the House, or helps his friends, and if he has told us anything, they are perfectly welcome to the information.
May I ask the minister if in the increased expenditure he includes the salaries of the people employed to go around the drug stores and see if the war tax measure is being enforced?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Yes.

If that be so, and if there is such an increase, it was unnecessary for

my hon. friend the Minister of Finance to get wrathy about the accusations made by the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lem-ieux), 'when he said there might be some election game in it. I was very much surprised when I saw the hon. minister get somewhat heated over it. May I give an example of what is taking place? In the city of Three Rivers where I live, they had an officer who came and bought Blue Jay corn plasters from eight or nine drug stores. Next morning the proprietors of the stores had summonses to appear before the magistrate. Now all the gentlemen who keep drug stores in Three Rivers are not of the same political complexion, some of them are Tories, some are Grits. So far as the Tories were concerned, this officer seemed to forget the war was on, because while all the Grits were before the magistrate not one Tory came. I went to court and put the question to this officer as to how he happened to forget the defeated candidate in the last Three Rivers election and did not buy any Blue Jay corn plasters from him. I may state here that these men were not drug store keepers, not druggists properly speaking. They sold patent medicines, toilet articles, etc. They did not know there was a chemical composition in this corn plaster, and advantage was taken of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Will my hon. friend permit a question? If this additional expenditure for preventive officers was intended to promote the interests of the Government at,the coming election, is my hon. friend aware that those estimates were brought down before an extension of term of Parliament was denied by the other side of this House? Ifhe hon member for Rouville says that the intention of this item was to engage preventive officers to assist in the coming election. On this side of the House we have not wanted any election, and when those estimates were brought down there was no election in view.
That is not an answer. We knew public opinion wanted a general election. If the Minister of Finance was asleep, we were not. Every one was clamoring for a general election.
Only in Quebec.

This "only in Quebec" business is played out. The difference is that in Quebec people speak their minds and you daren't. 'Go outside of Quebec and you will find that the hypocrites, when they get behind the door to make their mark will not make it for "no election;" and they will not make it for conscription 
either. The Minister of Finance is quite a financier, but he has given an explanation here which I do not quite understand. He justifies greater expenditure because we get greater revenue from the Customs Department. May I ask if it takes a man more time to figure out fifty per cent than it does to figure out twenty-five per cent? If you increase the duty from ten per cent to twenty per cent, does the minister say that will justify the doubling of the staff of the Customs Department?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What about the increased volume of business?
My hon. friend spoke of the increased revenue. He said the revenue from the Customs Department was greater.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Increased revenue comes from increased volume of business.

It comes from increased duty also. Let me come back to my Three Rivers merchants. Will the Minister of Inland Revenue tell me what instructions he gives those gentlemen when they start out	on work of that kind? Is
there a regulation to the effect that they are to protect all the Tories, and haul up .all the Grits, or are there any special instructions given? I would also like to know where he gets his men, who recommends them, and how they are appointed? If I have to see $55,000 of .an ip-creased vote passed to get a party a lot of political friends I want to know how they proceed.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I have before me a memorandum showing that in Three Rivers proceedings were taken against: A. Beli-veau, .P. Dufresne, C. Kleiner, M. Nassif, Pharmacie Pelletier, Pharmacie Williams, A. Boisseau, E. Briere, E. DesBois, Genest and Cloutier, E. Moise, C. Prince and R. O. Dumont.
What about the Pharmacie Normand, the proprietor of which was the Tory candidate in 1911?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: There was no report to my department against the Pharmacie Nor-mand. At present we have six cases pending, and seven others resulted in a fine of $50 each. There was no exception.
I may tell my hon. friend that the people who paid the $50 pleaded guilty, and there are no cases pending in Three Rivers. The other complaints were dismissed.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: When were they dismissed?
When they were tried.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: When was that?

At the time you summoned them. You know the date. It was during the course of last spring. That very same day11 sent a man to buy some Blue Jay corn plasters at the Pharmacie Nor-mand, .and there were no war stamps on it. My hon. friend's officer was not aware of that.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: In that case the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) failed in his duty.
There is no use in my hon. friend talking that way. He is not in Dorchester now.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The next time my hon. friend goes to the Pharmacie Normand and finds they do not put stamps on articles which should be stamped, if he will take it up with me, we will institute proceedings right away.

The men employed by the Minister of Inland Revenue were apparently unable to find Mr. Normand's place of business. I forget the exact reason why the other cases were dismissed. I believe it was because of some technicality in the laying of the complaints. Proper instructions were not given to the officers, and the informations were badly laid.* I believe that w.as why the actions were dismissed. Those who paid the $50 pleaded guilty to not having put the stamp on these Blue Jay corn plasters.
All Grits?

They were all Grits.
There were four other stores but they were not brought up. I do not know why, unless it was that they were Tories.
I suppose the Tories put the stamps on?

I tell you they did not. I went around myself, got the stuff, and there were no stamps on it. The Tories are being protected by my hon. friend. It need not bring such a laugh to my hon. friend the Minister of Finance or such-a broad . smile to the faces of my hon. friends opposite. It is an absolute fact. It is only by deeds of the past that we are enabled to judge what will take place in the future, especially with an election pending.

Assuming that the statement of my hon. friend from Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) is true, and that the hon. Minister
of Inland Revenue has been showing partiality to the Conservatives in Quebec, I feel that I have a grievance against the minister, for in the part of the country from which I come the proceedings that were taken against merchants for infringements of this Aot happened to have been taken against Conservatives.
They are too far away from the minister; he cannot keep his eye on them.
Upon what system are these employees, these informers, paid for laying these complaints and for travelling around the country?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: They get half the fine.
Do they get a salary apart from getting half the fine?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Yes, $900; too small in my judgment.
In cases where prosecutions are not proceeded with under orders from the department, do they get any portion of the amount that they would have received had the case gone on?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: They receive nothing except their pay.'
In that case who pays the travelling expenses?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: In many cases, when it is a first offence, and when an affidavit is sent to the department stating that there was no intention to disobey the law, we are not severe, and I think my hon. friend knows it himself.	[DOT]

My hon. friend has said
that in some cases where an affidavit is sent by the person complained against to the effect that he had no intention of disobeying the law and that it was only an occasional infraction, the department have remitted the fine on payment of costs. What becomes of the costs in those cases where his own political friends are not proceeded against?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
In all such cases the
costs are paid by the defendant. In the two oases that are very well known to my hon. friend from Sheftord, that is what happened.

For the benefit of my hon. friend from Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) I have explained the case of two friends in whose behalf I applied to the department in connection with a fine. In those two

cases the fine was not collected when an affidavit was filed to the effect that the violation was not intentional, that it was not customary, that the sale was made by a young employee during the absence of the merchant. In those eases the fine was not collected, but the costs were collected. Who paid the costs in the case of the complaint laid against Mr. Welch, druggist, of Waterloo, where the complaint was withdrawn? Were any costs paid by the defendant Mr. Welch who happened to be a Conservative?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I will inquire about this special case.
It will be very interesting to the electors of Shefford, especially those who have paid their fines.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
Who was representing
Mr. Welch?
I think that Mr. Davidson, the defeated Conservative candidate, represented Mr. Welch.
Is he a lawyer?

He is not a lawyer, but [DOT]
he administers the patronage in Shefford county.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Is Mr. Davidson a lawyer?

He is not a lawyer, but
the case never went into court.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Then there would be no costs?

There was the cost of
making the complaint, of reporting it to the collector at Sherbrooke, of sending notices from Sherbrooke to Ottawa and the salary and travelling expenses of the officer.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
Unless they were paid
by Mr. Davidson.

They possibly may have
been paid by Mr. Davidson, but I have my doubts about it.

I understand from the
minister that half the fine goes to the informer or excise officer?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Yes.
And that man gets besides $900 a year?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Yes.
Plus travelling expenses? Mr. SEVIGNY: Yes.
Does the minister think that it is the proper way of administering his department to give the informer half of the fine? And will he givq us the reasons for that policy?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: It is considered by the department the only effective way. It is nothing new. You will see it done every day in our province under the license law.
Not half.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I do not know exactly *what the amount is.

Officers under the license law get fifteen per cent. They used to get half the fine but they are doing away with that. What can one think of the minister's statement that the only effective way of carrying on the administration of the department is to give fifty per cent of the fine to the informer? I think that to give $900 to the man who does what this mam did in Three Rivers, plus his travelling expenses, is overpaying him unless the money is to be turned over to the Dorchester election fund or some other fund unknown to the House. You cannot get men who will go around and fish for information for "half the fine, and if you do, you get a class of men who are mot a credit to the department. If you have a good officer and if his salary is not sufficient, raise it. Out of this $57,000 that is being asked for by the minister, there should be enough to raise the salaries of each of these officers to such a point that it will be possible for him to live and do his duty.
I do not believe in giving the informer one half of the fine because those who will do that are generally not the class of men required for this sort of duty. If 'they were paid a salary and travelling expenses I think the Government should get the benefit of - all fines collected.

How much was paid
to the informer at Three Rivers during the last twelve months?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Seven people were fined $50 each; that would mean $175 to the informer.
The minister says there are other cases pending. What are they?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The cases of A. Belineau, P. Dufresne, C. Kleiner, M. Nassif, Phar-macie Pelletier, Pharmacie Williams.
Has there been any report to the department about these cases?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Not yet.
When were the complaints made?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: During last spring.

Is not the minister aware that all those cases were dismissed by the magistrate last spring at the time the others pleaded guilty?
Mr. SEVTGiNY: We have no report from the lawyer.

I will not make a report, it is not my duty. To whom was the 5175 paid?
Mr. SEVIGiNY:	I think to Mr. Hardy,
of Quebec.

Has any inquiry been
made by the department about the cases now under advisement before the court?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Probably.

What is the probability
and what was the kind of inquiry? Probably it will rain to-morrow.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
This matter is handled
by the secretary of the department, .and we have confidence in our lawyer. When we send a case to a lawyer we ihave confidence in him, and we are waiting for the report.
That is not an explanation. A client generally inquires of his lawyer how his case is progressing.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: That is what we do.
Those cases were all tried at the same time and some pleaded guilty.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Were you there at the time?
I was there in Court last spring, and the cases were dismissed because the informations were not properly laid. Why did the minister not inquire about the cases?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Were you there when the others were fined?
The cases were never tried, the defendants deposited their $50.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: And were the cases of those fined pleaded at the same time as those dismissed?

I have sat here for seventeen years, and this is the first time I have heard a minister o ill on the Opposition to give him information about his estimates. The minister does not find it worth while to look after this business, after bringing practically all the men in
a particular business in the town into Court. There has been ample time for the minister to get reports about status of the cases.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I do not quite understand my hon. friend. He stages that these cases have been dismissed and at the same time that some of the parties were fined.
They pleaded guilty.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
They
pleaded guilty and have been fined $50. Once more my hon. friend* maintains that these cases have been dismissed, whereas from the reports in the department, they would still be under advisement. How could we have a report stating that seven parties . have been fined $50 as provided by the Act, and no report concerning the cases which, according to my hon. friend, have been dismissed?

I see the
point that the minister is trying to make.
I will answer him in English.
The minister asks how it is he has received the money when fines were imposed and that he has no further report about the cases dismissed. That is just the question I am asking the minister. He has been derelict in his duty if he does not know what was done in these cases.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: My hon. friend says the cases were dismissed, and my answer is that the cases were not dismissed.
All right.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: And the information we have in my department is that the cases are pending.
When did the minister get the last report on these cases?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I am sorry, I have not the date before me tonight.
How is it he has let the cases drag on since February last without asking for a report?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: We have asked for reports. We have many cases, not only in Three Rivers and Quebec, but all over the country. We follow them as well as we can, and we ask for reports. We have every confidence in the lawyers who represent us.

Does the hon. minister
want the House and the country to- believe that, when a case is taken in the. month of February, and he receives fines from a certain number of cases tried at the same time, and asks for a report concerning the other case, and there is no report received up to July, he is going to continue his confidence in that attorney, and to continue to entrust the business of the country to him?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: My hon. friend knows very well that if you take an action say in Montreal, it may come before the court three years from now.

If my hon. friend had practised law as much as he wishes us to believe we would know that there is a great deal of difference in cases before a Superior Court and cases before a district magistrate. A case may drag along in the Superior Court in Montreal for years, but a case before a district magistrate does not drag along for two or three months or two or three weeks in any place in the country. There is no congestion in the district magistrate's court.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: How long did the Lepage case continue in my hon. friend's own district? My hon. friend knows that it was about a year.

My hon. friend knows that the Lepage case had nothing to do with the administration of his department, and it would be altogether too long to- explain to this House and the country the good fortune that attended Mr. Lepage in his liberation from the jail, through the good offices of the present Minister of Inland Revenue.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Under the hon. gentleman's recommendation.

Yes, it was asked for by the minister. The Lepage preliminary inquiry did not take a year, or six months, or two months. It was over in a month. Lepage was condemned to stand his trial. He remained under bonds for practically three years, awaiting a term of the Court of King's Bench. And when that term was held he refused to come before the court. He obtained an order for speedy trial before the district magistrate, and- after that the trial was over inside of six weeks. Why did not the minister ask for a report in those cases at Three Rivers? Upon what date did my hon. friend rechive the fine in the cases in Three Rivers?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
The date is not mentioned here.
CM. Sevignv.]

I rose to ask a question a little while ago, and I think it is very important information for the House. What amount has been collected by the

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I will add it up.
I am perfectly willing that it should be brought down later. I thought it would be a good thing for the country to know.

The last night we discussed the hon. minister's estimate [DOT] I brought to his notice certain correspondence that took place between his department and the Auditor General. This correspondence is found on pages 37, 38 and 39 of the fir=t volume of the Auditor General's Report for the last fiscal year. In the correspondence the Auditor General complains that the department has been employing temporary assistance without complying with the law. The Minister of Finance told us that every thing in connection with the employment of men in the hon. minister's department is performed with mathematical accuracy, on chronometer time, and that being so, I am surprised that the Auditor General found it necessary to engage the attention of the department in many cases to find out how it was that some eleven men, as appears on page 38 of this correspondence, were employed without any apparent authority, or without complying with any regulation. I understood the hon. Minister of Finance to say to-night, in the language of the law, which he was throwing around the Minister of Inland Revenue, that that very learned and responsible body, the Treasury Board, had to have a hand in this before anybody was appointed.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: What is the date?

The date of the letter is the 21st December, 1915. This is the latest report of the Auditor General, and up to the end of this correspondence no satisfactory answer is given why those men were taken on without authority and retained without any authority. I did not press this inquiry on the former occasion, because the minister could not be expected to know at the time, but that is now. nearly a month ago. Perhaps the minister forgot that I brought this matter up on that occasion. I was promised some information in regard to it. I find on page 1-39 of this

volume what appears to me to be an irregularity in view of the high standard set in these matters by the Minister of Finance. I find this letter:
Audit Office, November 15, 1916.
Sir,-I have again to call your attention to the correspondence between your department and this office in regard to the employment of Mr. J. A. Cantin as a temporary excise officer. The objection taken was that he could not be properly employed except under the authority of an order in council.
The only action I can find that has been taken was his transfer to the position of temporary acting inspector of electricity at Quebec at the same salary of $1,400.
Was that appointment made by order in council and has he passed the necessary examination prescribed by section 11 of the Electricity Inspection Act of 1907, which states that the Governor in Council may appoint inspectors or assistant inspectors, but not until they havo passed a qualifying examination?
I am, sir, your obedient servant,
E. D. Sutherland, for A. G. The Deputy Minister of Inland Revenue.
I find on 17th November, 1916, this answer from the Department of Inland Revenue:
Dear Mr. Sutherland,-I have your letter of November 16, concerning Mr. J. A. Cantin, Acting Inspector of Electricity at Quebec, at the salary of $1,400 per year.
I may say that Mr. Cantin is a very efficient officer, and has been preparing for his examination ever since he has been transferred to the Gas and Electricity Branch. He will be in position to pass this examination about the 15th of January next, when his position will be rectified.
Hoping this will be satisfactory.
This letter is signed by the deputy minister. Mr.. Sutherland replies to that on 21st November, 1916, stating that the explanation is not at all satisfactory. There is scarcely a young man in Canada but would be glad to join the Civil Service and then attend some educational institution in which he would prepare for an examination while being paid at the rate of $1,400 per annum. The explanation given here is not satisfactory.
The reason for passing the Civil Service Act is that men shall join the Civil Service only after they have properly qualified. When inquiry is made in regard to the matter I have mentioned, not by a party who might be captious about these matters, not by a man like myself who might be trying to find fault, but by the Auditor General, the only explanation given him is that there is a young man, or an old man, or whatever he may be, attending school for the purpose of passing an examination, and in the meantime he is receiving $1,400 a
year from the department, without the slightest pretext on the part of the minister of complying with the Civil Service Act. At all events, there is no pretext to be found in the explanation given by the deputy minister. When these estimates were before the committee on a former occasion I .asked for, and was promised, an explanation. I may say, not only to the Minister of Inland Revenue, but to every minister in the Government, that there is a great deal of complaint about the infraction of the Civil Service Act, .and the criticism is made that the Government apparently consider it is really on the statute book for the purpose of being violated and evaded rather than observed. It would be much better to throw the thing open .altogether than have the farce or pretext of a Civil Service Act when the Act is not observed, when not the slightest attention is paid to it. When it suits the minister to make room for a friend, that friend comes in; he is paid a salary, and the explanation is given that he is at school somewhere, .and while he is at school he is getting .a salary. That is not good government; it is not fair to the people, who, ,at their own expense, are studying in order to pass .the examination, that others should be permitted to become qualified at the expense of the Government and be placed in positions which they do not deserve and for which they have not the required qualifications under the law. I protest against such things, and I hope they will be remedied, and that we shall not be met with such conduct as this again. I hold responsible for this line of action the Minister of Finance, .as he is, ex-officio, a member of the Treasury Board. He told us that not only had we the Apdi-tor General and the head of the department, but we had this higher and stronger protection, this great bulwark for the protection of the people, the Treasury Board, of which he himself is the head and front- but over his head evidently goes this man with his $1,400 a year, although he has not [DOT] the slightest pretext of qualification for the position. I would invite the Minister of Finance to make another eloquent speech in the endeavour to explain away this situation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is too late and too hot.
The Minister of Finance speaks with such vim and absolute disregard for time or hot weather.

asking for .an increase of $26,000 in the Weights and Measures branch. speechtext:
The actual expenditure

It is estimated that the department will need the amount asked for this year -as travelling expenses have been steadily increasing, and as the branch is developing constantly to keep p-ace with the industrial .activities of

the country, as is evidenced in the increased fees collected for the l-ast three years as follows:	Fees collected in 1915,

And my hon. friend proipoises to .spend $25,000 more for the sake of that $20,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: This branch is not considered by the department as a revenue producer, but a -service that is run in the interest of the public.
Why are you putting it forward, then, as a revenue producer?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I quoted the fees collected merely as an evidence of the increased work the department is doing.

Does my hon. friend really attempt to say that it is going to cost this country $25,000 more in order that the officials of the Weights and Measures branch may collect $20,000 more fees all over the country? It would not take the officials of the department ten minutes to collect that $20,000 if it was scattered all over the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: To illustrate how the work of the department is increasing, last year we had to examine 300 more elevator scales in the West than the year previous. This service is run in the interest of the public. The officers must be paid their salaries and travelling expenses, and the only reason we are asking for an increase is that the service is expanding.

My hon. friend says that there was an expenditure of $73,000 last year, which was $8,000 more than the vote. On June 15, in answer to a question in the House as to this increase, he said:
We were given $65,000 last year by Parliament, but we were short by $15,000, and it is to cover that deficit that we are asking for $15,000 more this year.
Now my hon. friend tells us that it was not $15,000 more than they spent last year, but only $8,000 more; still he asks for $15,000 when the over-expenditure last year, according to the written statement he gave, was only $8,000. What is he going to do with the other $7,000?
'Mr. SEVIGNY:	These estimates -were
prepared in November last, before the end of the fiscal year, and at the time we had not an exact idea as to how we should come out. Our total expenditure last year was

$73,229, and it is figured that the amount required in my department this year will be about $80,000.

The explanation
about these estimates being prepared last November has no relevancy at all to the matter. On 15th' June my hon. friend told me that the over-expenditure was $15,000; to-night he tells us it is only $8,000. It was on account of the fact that the overexpenditure was said to be $15,000 that he attempted to justify asking for $15,000 more. If the hon. minister wanted to pay the slightest attention to economy, upon what principle does he attempt to get $7,000 more for a service when he would be amply in funds to provide for it, according to his prepared and written statement to-night, with $73,000 instead of $80,000? My hon. friend need not speak about the Estimates having been prepared in November. On 15th June, with his deputy sitting beside him, and after the financial year had ended, he told us it was $15,000; now on reflection he finds it is only $8,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I can assure my hon. friend that economy is practised in my department. I must say that generally speaking the officers in the department are underpaid, considering the high cost of living. This applies particularly to the officers in the Outside Service.
Don't they get half of the fines?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue

Every day I receive requests for increases in salary, and it is my intention to go before the Minister of Finance shortly and ask him to increase those salaries. We have practised economy to such an extent that we now realize that our officers are not sufficiently paid.

My hon. friend is
coming back to that again, and is giving us this homily aiborut salaries. We are not talking about salaries at all. We are now discussing rent, fuel, travelling expenses, and stationery. Not a cent of that is salaries. It is simply an extravagance of $8,-
000.	The minister could facilitate the passage of his estimates if he would decrease this item by $7,000, which, according to his statement, is surplusage.

It would be a pleasure
to me if I could decrease it, but I am informed by the officers of my department,

I have been a member of Parliament for a good many years, and I never saw any minister come here with evidence of such incompetenoy in his department as the minister has shown here on the two occasions he has come to the point. Either be is absolutely incompetent himself, or his officials are incompetent. How does the minister explain the fact that a month ago he told us he had spent $15,000, and on that basis he asked for $15,000, and now he comes and says he spent $8,000, and although he only spent $8,000 he wants $15,-
000.	In justification of that he says, " We collected $20,000 more in fees"-and the next moment he says he wants to increase the salaries of his officials. My hon. friend has shown clearly in his own statement that he is asking for $7,000 for which there is no necessity under competent administration, and he ought to reduce the vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue

Provisional allowance of not more than $150 each to officers in Manitoba and provinces west thereof, whose salaries from any government service do not exceed $2,500 .	.	.	$11,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: It is considered that west of the Great Lakes the cost of living is higher than in the eastern provinces. This practice is followed not only in the Inland Revenue Department but also the Post Office Department.

I think it is absolutely unfair that officials in the western provinces should be given more than those in the eastern provinces. Living expenses are no higher in the West than in the East. Men living in the Maritime Provinces and Quebec are under the same expenses as those in the West.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
According to the' information we have in the department, the cost



of living is higher in the West than the East-(I am ready to admit that the cost of living is very high in the East too). It is for that reason that we grant this amount.

I have not yet been able to learn that the cost of living in the West is any higher than it is in the East. The time has arrived when preferences of this kind should he cut out, and officials all through the Dominion treated equally in regard to salaries, instead of a little gift and sop being given to officials in one portion of the Dominion while similar treatment is denied to others. Referring to the minister's reply to my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald), that it was his intention to give increased salaries to the Outside officials, it seems to me that the argument is not sufficient to justify this increase. Any hon. gentleman who has anything to do with patronage is always able to find numerous applications for any vacancies that occur. It is easy to get applications for these positions from men who know what the salary is, and therefore the argument in that regard does not afford any answer to the question as .to why this increased vote is being asked for. Not only have we not found any difficulty in securing applications to fill these vacancies, but my experience has been that we have too many applications. The minister would be starting out in the right direction if he would put all the officials in his department in the same position, give them equal salaries, and cut out this gift of $150 to western officials.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I can promise my hon. friend that I will give my best consideration to his remarks.

In Nova Scotia the Department of Education -and our superintendents of education do not give any recognition practically to the metric system. There has been some agitation in favour of it.
